title: Kendall v. United States ex rel. Stokes (1838)
shortTitle: Kendall v. United States ex rel. Stokes (1838)
summary: A court may issue mandamus to compel an executive officer to perform a purely ministerial duty that Congress has imposed, and the President has no power to forbid its performance.
notes:
Key line: "To contend that the obligation imposed on the President to see the laws faithfully executed, implies a power to forbid their execution, is a novel construction of the constitution, and entirely inadmissible." (Thompson, J.)

Citation: 37 U.S. (12 Pet.) 524 (1838).

sections.Parties: The relators were William B. Stokes and his partners in the firm of Stockton and Stokes, contractors who carried the mail for the Post Office Department. The plaintiff in error was Amos Kendall, Postmaster General of the United States, who had refused to credit them with the full amount of an award made under an act of Congress. The suit was brought in the name of the United States on the relation of Stokes and his partners against Kendall in his official capacity. Kendall defended on the ground that he answered only to the President for the performance of his duties, so that no court could direct him.
sections.Material Facts: Stockton and Stokes held mail contracts under which the previous Postmaster General had allowed them extra credits. When Kendall took office he reexamined the contracts, struck the allowances and recharged the contractors with payments they had received. The contractors petitioned Congress, which passed a special act on July 2, 1836. The act directed the Solicitor of the Treasury, Virgil Maxcy, to settle the claims on principles of equity and directed the Postmaster General to credit the contractors with whatever sum the Solicitor found due. Maxcy awarded about $161,563. Kendall credited only about $122,101 and refused to credit the remaining $39,462. A Senate Judiciary Committee report and a unanimous Senate resolution said the award was final and should be paid. Kendall still refused.
sections.Procedural History: The relators petitioned the Circuit Court of the United States for the District of Columbia for a writ of mandamus commanding Kendall to credit them with the full award. After proceedings in that court, it issued a peremptory mandamus. Kendall took a writ of error to the Supreme Court. He argued that the case was an attempt to control an executive officer who was subject only to the direction of the President, and that in any event the circuit court of the District lacked power to issue mandamus to a federal officer, relying on M'Intire v. Wood and M'Cluny v. Silliman. The Supreme Court heard the case in the January Term of 1838 and affirmed the judgment.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, could a court compel the Postmaster General by mandamus to credit the contractors with the amount awarded by the Solicitor of the Treasury, or was the Postmaster General answerable only to the President because of the President's constitutional duty to take care that the laws be faithfully executed? Second, if mandamus was a proper remedy, did the circuit court for the District of Columbia, unlike the circuit courts sitting in the states, have jurisdiction and authority to issue the writ against an officer of the United States?
sections.Holding: The Court affirmed. The act of Congress required the Postmaster General to perform a precise, definite and purely ministerial act about which he had no discretion, and neither he nor the President had authority to refuse it. Mandamus was the fit remedy because the right was established by positive law, the duty was clear and specific, and no other remedy was adequate. The circuit court of the District of Columbia had authority to issue the writ because the common law of Maryland, including the writ of mandamus, had been adopted for the District, so that court possessed powers the circuit courts in the states did not.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Thompson wrote that the case did not interfere with any executive function. Executive officers are not under the exclusive direction of the President for every duty. Congress may impose duties on an executive officer that are not repugnant to the Constitution, and when the duty is ministerial it is subject to the control of the law, not the direction of the President. The claim that the Take Care Clause let the President stop the payment would vest in him a dispensing power over legislation and paralyze the administration of justice. The Court noted that the President had in fact disclaimed any such power and had referred the matter to Congress. The act left the Postmaster General no discretion over the Solicitor's decision, and the Senate's resolutions confirmed the award. The alternative remedies suggested at the bar, application to Congress, removal of the officer, or an action for damages, were all inadequate. Turning to jurisdiction, the Court explained that M'Intire v. Wood and M'Cluny v. Silliman denied the circuit courts in the states the power to issue mandamus only because Congress had not delegated that judicial power to them, not because the Constitution forbade it. The District of Columbia was different: the Act of 1801 continued Maryland's common law in force there, and that law included the prerogative writ of mandamus, so the circuit court of the District could issue it against a federal officer.

topics.lrs-o-ministerial-duties: A required payment could not be withheld under presidential direction; faithful execution does not imply power to forbid execution.
topics.lrs-n-discrete-required-action: Kendall's mandamus to compel a ministerial statutory duty is the historical root of APA § 706(1) relief for discrete, legally required action.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was 6 to 3. Chief Justice Taney dissented, agreeing that the duty was ministerial but concluding that the circuit court of the District of Columbia had no statutory authority to issue a mandamus to a federal officer. Justice Barbour wrote a separate dissent on the same jurisdictional ground, reasoning that adopting Maryland's common law could give the court no greater power than Maryland's own courts had, and they could not issue mandamus to a federal officer. Justice Catron concurred in the opinions of the Chief Justice and Justice Barbour.
